title: Vanilla Agentic Framework
subtitle: A Blueprint Guide for Building an Enterprise Agentic Platform with Best Practices Built In
author: shivank.sharma@wipro.com
footer: Vanilla Agentic Framework — Blueprint Guide · shivank.sharma@wipro.com

sections.heading: Preface
body: This document is a blueprint guide for teams who want to build an agentic framework: a platform where AI agents, orchestrated as durable state machines, execute reusable skills inside ephemeral, sandboxed runners and produce versioned, reviewable artifacts.

The framework described here is deliberately domain-agnostic. To keep the concepts concrete, the guide uses four neutral example skills — Research, Planning, Execution, and Reporting — but these are placeholders: any domain can plug its own skills into the same pipeline without changing the framework itself.

Every component maps to a managed Azure platform service, so the blueprint can be stood up without inventing infrastructure. All architecture diagrams and flowcharts referenced in the text are embedded in the relevant chapters.
This is an architecture-phase document: it defines boundaries, contracts, and a build order. It deliberately contains no application source code.

sections.heading: Target Audience
body: - Platform and solution architects designing an agentic system on top of LangGraph and Deep Agents
- Engineering leads who need clear microservice boundaries, data ownership, and a phased build order before writing code
- Teams evaluating how AI agents can research a problem, propose a plan, and act on it with human oversight
- FinOps and governance stakeholders who need cost-per-run visibility and human-in-the-loop control points
- Azure practitioners who want a component-to-service mapping for deploying the framework on managed Azure services

sections.heading: Introduction
body: An agentic framework is more than a chatbot with tools. It is a platform with five concerns kept deliberately separate: how users reach it (access), what the agents know (skills and knowledge), how work is orchestrated and executed (orchestration and execution), how quality and cost are measured (evaluation), and how the stakeholders who own the outcome stay engaged (engagement).

The Vanilla Agentic Framework realizes these concerns as independently deployable microservices behind a single gateway. Agents are built with LangGraph (durable state machines with checkpoints and human-in-the-loop pauses) and Deep Agents (planning and sub-agent fan-out). Work never executes on the control plane: every skill runs inside an ephemeral runner that is created on demand, receives its skills by mounting, and is destroyed afterwards.
Three design commitments define the framework:

- Skills are centralized, versioned content — prompts and procedures managed in a registry (Langfuse), never baked into runner images. A dedicated service, the skill-loader, mounts them onto runners at execution time.

- Every skill execution produces a durable, versioned artifact. The pipeline composes these artifacts into a final deliverable — the Final Deliverable Document. There is no merge request or pull request anywhere in the process.

- Everything is anchored on an Engagement ID — a generic unit of work — not a git repository. The platform is interactive: users collaborate with agents through a guided wizard rather than waiting on batch jobs.

Four example skills carry the reference pipeline: Research (gather and confirm context), Planning (analyze and recommend), Execution (carry out the approved plan), and Reporting (summarize outcomes). Swap in your own domain skills and the framework is unchanged.

sections.heading: Architecture at a Glance
body: The framework is organized into six logical layers. Each layer contains a small number of microservices with a single, clear responsibility, and clients only ever talk to the gateway.

table.caption: The six layers and their responsibilities
rows: Single edge: auth, RBAC, REST + SSE
Job lifecycle and agent state machines
Skills registry, org facts, episodic memory
Traces, quality signals, cost per run

image.caption: Layered architecture with Azure service icons — request, mount, and event flows across the six layers

body: The control plane (gateway, job-service, agent-orchestrator, skill-loader, sandbox-provisioner) is always on and holds all credentials. The data plane (ephemeral runners) exists only for the duration of a skill execution and never holds long-lived secrets.

sections.heading: End-to-End Process
body: A run begins when a user opens an engagement on the platform by its Engagement ID. From there the default pipeline is sequential: Research, Planning, a human approval gate, Execution, and finally Reporting. Each skill persists an artifact, and after the last skill the platform composes the Final Deliverable Document from all of them.

The workflow is hybrid rather than rigid: any skill can be re-run if its inputs changed, or skipped when its previous artifact is still valid. The single mandatory human gate sits after Planning, before any irreversible execution takes place.

image.caption: Overall process — all layers, the four skills, artifacts, HITL gate, FinOps and Adaption engines on one canvas

body: The flow below isolates the skill pipeline itself: four skills, four artifacts, one approval gate, one final document. Cost events stream to the FinOps engine and lifecycle events notify stakeholders through the Adaption engine.

body: Shared infrastructure completes the picture:
- Postgres + pgvector — structured domain data plus embeddings for semantic and episodic memory
- Langfuse — procedural skill prompts (draft / staging / production labels) plus agent tracing
- Message bus — durable job and event fan-out, decoupling the pipeline from downstream consumers
- Runner workspace store — a per-job share where runners write artifacts

sections.heading: System Runtime View
body: At runtime the framework separates into an always-on control plane and an on-demand data plane. The gateway is the single edge; job-service owns the job's truth; agent-orchestrator drives LangGraph graphs; skill-loader and sandbox-provisioner manage the fleet of ephemeral runners.

image.caption: System overview — control plane, data plane, and shared stores at runtime

body: The gateway exposes an engagement-centric API. Every route is anchored on the Engagement ID, which keeps the UI, MCP tools, and CLI at exact parity:
- POST /engagements/{id}/research — start or continue the guided Research wizard
- POST /engagements/{id}/plan — run Planning
- POST /engagements/{id}/approve — the HITL gate on the plan
- POST /engagements/{id}/execute and /report — the two downstream skills
- GET /engagements/{id}/jobs/{job_id}/artifacts — list and fetch skill artifacts
- GET /engagements/{id}/jobs/{job_id}/final-deliverable — the final composed document
- GET /engagements/{id}/costs and /track — FinOps and engagement views
Illustrative RBAC roles: viewer, operator, skill-author, skill-reviewer, admin, finops-viewer.

sections.heading: Skill & Knowledge Layer
body: Skills are the framework's unit of capability. Procedural skill content lives in Langfuse prompt management under draft / staging / production labels; metadata, organizational facts, and episodes live in Postgres + pgvector behind the knowledge-service.

image.caption: Skill & knowledge platform — registry, memory stores, and the reviewed skill-update loop

table.caption: The four example skills
rows: Guided gathering and confirmation of context for the engagement
Analyze findings, score options, recommend a course of action
Carry out the approved plan against enterprise systems

body: Optional secondary skills can be added per domain; each emits its own artifact and still produces no merge request.

table.caption: Three memory types
rows: How to research / plan / execute / report
Org facts: standards, catalogs, policies, reference data

body: The knowledge base improves itself under governance: completed jobs write episodes, a reflection step opens change requests, a human skill-reviewer approves, and the change publishes to Langfuse or updates semantic facts. Rollback is simply re-pointing the Langfuse production label.

sections.heading: Execution Layer — Ephemeral Runners & Skill Mounting
body: The execution layer enforces the framework's strongest rule: skills are never baked into images and agents never fetch registry content themselves. The skill-loader is the central mount authority.

image.caption: Execution layer — skill-loader resolves, spawns, and mounts; agents consume mounted skills

body: For each phase the sequence is: the orchestrator asks skill-loader to prepare a runtime for a skill key; skill-loader resolves the production skill content, facts, and episodes from knowledge-service and Langfuse; it asks sandbox-provisioner to spawn an ephemeral runner; it mounts the skill bundle onto that runner; and only then do agents execute, using exactly the skills mounted for that run.

table.caption: Runner types
rows: Skill 1 — data gathering, enrichment, findings writes
Skill 3 — enterprise system APIs, action execution

body: Runners are destroyed on completion or TTL expiry; a sweeper reclaims orphans. One workspace exists per job, with no cross-job leakage. The sandbox backend is a protocol seam: local Docker first, managed Kubernetes pods later, with no change to agent code.

sections.heading: Interactive Guided Wizard
body: Research is a guided collaboration, not a silent batch pull. The user opens an engagement, and the agent walks the relevant context with them step by step, enriching with live checks where available. The user confirms the result before it becomes the Research Findings Artifact.

image.caption: Guided wizard — user and agent converge on confirmed findings

body: Wizard progress is checkpointed in LangGraph, so an abandoned session resumes exactly where it stopped; the UI receives progress over server-sent events. An abandoned wizard also triggers an engagement nudge from the Adaption engine.

sections.heading: Artifact Pipeline & Final Deliverable
body: Every completed skill persists a versioned skill artifact. When the approved path completes, the platform composes the Final Deliverable Document from all artifacts. The document is a first-class, downloadable deliverable in the UI — there is no git merge anywhere in the process.

image.caption: Artifact flow — four skill artifacts compose into the Final Deliverable Document

body: Artifact metadata lives with job-service and knowledge-service; payloads live in the runner workspace or object store.

sections.heading: FinOps Engine
body: The FinOps engine answers one question with authority: what did this agent run cost — per job, per engagement, per skill, per day?

image.caption: FinOps engine — ingesting traces and runner lifetimes into cost records and rollups

body: It ingests Langfuse spans (tokens, model, latency) keyed by job, phase, skill, and agent; attributes ephemeral runner compute when metered; persists an immutable cost_record; and exposes rollups through the gateway. Soft budgets and alerts are optional additions.
A cost_record carries: id, job_id, engagement_id, skill_key, phase, agent_id, token_input, token_output, model_cost, runner_cost, total_cost, currency, recorded_at.

Deployment notes: it is an independently deployable service that exclusively owns cost_record; both ingest paths are asynchronous, so FinOps downtime never blocks a job; it scales on ingest volume, not job volume.

sections.heading: Adaption Engine
body: The Adaption engine keeps each engagement moving. It tracks progress per engagement and emails stakeholders at the moments that matter — approvals waiting, wizards abandoned, deadlines approaching.

image.caption: Adaption engine — lifecycle events become tracked engagements and audited stakeholder emails

table.caption: Example triggers
rows: Ask stakeholder to review and approve the plan

body: An engagement track carries: engagement_id, stage, stakeholder_emails, last_contact_at, next_action, sla_due_at, status. Emails are audited as email_event records.

Deployment notes: the engine consumes job lifecycle events from the message bus, so the pipeline never waits on email; the mail transport (Graph, SMTP, or a provider) sits behind one interface; a separate scheduler component sweeps SLA and idle timers.

sections.heading: Design Principles
body: The framework's choices follow a small set of principles that generalize across domains:

table.caption: Design principles and how the framework applies them
rows: Microservices with clear APIs; swap Docker for K8s runners behind one protocol
Gateway replicas; workers scale on queue depth; runners on demand
Agent logic is cloud-agnostic; infrastructure bindings are pluggable
REST + MCP + CLI; skills are prompts and SKILL.md content, not binaries
Approval after Planning; skill-review for knowledge updates
Orchestrator on the control plane; work in runners; credentials stay central
Fan-out within phases; many jobs across workers
FIFO pipeline, circular revise loops, fan-out / consolidate, handoff-to-human
Job DB, LangGraph checkpoints, runner workspace, knowledge, traces, cost, engagement

sections.heading: Build Order & Roadmap
body: The architecture phase — microservice map, this guide, and the diagram set — is complete. Implementation proceeds in five phases, each delivering a usable increment:

table.caption: Implementation phases
rows: Gateway + job-service + Engagement entity + guided wizard skeleton + local Docker runner + Skill 1 end to end (Research Findings Artifact)
Planning skill + HITL gate + skill-loader + Langfuse skill registry integration
Execution + Reporting runners (Skills 3–4) + managed K8s ephemeral runner backend + Final Deliverable Document composition
knowledge-service memory (episodes, reflection, skill-review HITL) + MCP / CLI parity
finops-engine (cost records from traces + runner metrics) + adaption-engine (tracks + email) + dashboards

body: Open items to resolve during implementation: the concrete skill catalog for the first use case, live enrichment mechanisms per data source, plan scoring dimensions and weights, cloud provider bindings, the adaption email transport, and whether FinOps v1 includes runner compute cost or model cost only.

sections.heading: Conclusion
body: The Vanilla Agentic Framework shows that an agentic platform is, at its core, a disciplined separation of six concerns: access, orchestration, skills and knowledge, execution, evaluation, and engagement. Keep skills centralized and mounted at runtime, keep execution ephemeral and credential-free, make every step produce a durable artifact, and put a human gate in front of anything irreversible.

The four example skills — Research, Planning, Execution, Reporting — exercise every part of the framework: interactive wizards, scoring and recommendation, approval gates, real-world actions, cost accounting, and stakeholder engagement. Replacing them with skills from your own domain changes nothing structural.

With the microservice boundaries, contracts, diagrams, and build order in this guide, a team can proceed directly to Phase 1 scaffolding with confidence that the architecture will hold as the platform grows.
